maths.lane_summary: MATHEMATICAL CORRECTNESS lane. I re-derived each new statistic from scratch and checked the implementation against my derivation, then ran numerical experiments to confirm or refute every concern the brief raised. WHAT IS CORRECT (negative results, stated so nobody re-litigates them): (a) glm_contrast_z's pooled SE is algebraically exact — it reproduces scipy.stats.ttest_ind(equal_var=True) to 2.2e-16 at na/nb = 5/5, 4/12, 12/4, 2/30, 15/15, so ddof and the (na-1)/(nb-1) weighting are right; (b) detection_floor is sound — achieved_power is empirically monotone under common random numbers (no violations on a 0.05 grid over effect 0.60-1.60), re-seeding with the same seed IS correct CRN because numpy's normal(loc,...) consumes the same stream regardless of loc, the doubling loop brackets [hi/2, hi] so it cannot overshoot, it cannot return 0, and the returned floor matches the exact noncentral-t MDE adjusted for the rank test's 0.955 ARE to 0.2% at n=15 (1.0830 vs 1.0845) and 1.5% at n=24; the +8% at n=6 is genuine permutation discreteness, not a bug; (c) using mc_perm_p(n_perm=400) inside detection_floor instead of the exact enumeration perm_p dispatches to at n=6 costs at most 1 percentage point of power, so the floor does describe the test the verdict uses; (d) mean-of-z vs z-of-ROI-mean — for a uniform effect under homoscedastic equicorrelated noise the two have identical SNR to first order (both delta*sqrt(n/2)/(sigma*sqrt(rho+(1-rho)/V))), and mean-of-z is strictly better under heteroscedastic per-vertex noise, so there is NO power pathology from correlation; (e) the ndim branch in raw_roi_mean/roi_minus_reference has no latent bug — 1D and 2D agree exactly (2.0/2.0 and -52.5/-52.5 on matched inputs), 3D and 0D raise IndexError, a list raises AttributeError, and the overlap guard fires; (f) event_locked_contrast's mean-of-category-means matches its docstring and is the unbiased estimator of the equal-weight baseline (higher variance than pooling only at unequal exemplar counts, which is the intended trade); (g) 26/26 tests pass. WHAT IS WRONG: seven defects, one of which I rate critical. The headline is that glm_contrast_z uses a POOLED (equal-variance) standard error. That is exactly right at equal n and provably wrong at unequal n: at the S2 design shape (faces n=50 vs pooled other categories n=200, V=58 vertices, rho=0.6, 800 replicates, n_perm=400) the permutation test's Type I error is correctly calibrated at 0.0225 when the two conditions have equal across-exemplar sd, but rises to 0.0650 (2.6x nominal, 4.6 SE) at a modest 1.5:1 sd ratio and 0.125 (5x) at 3:1, and collapses to 0.0050 and then exactly 0.0000 in the other direction — a guaranteed NO-GO no matter how large the true effect. Swapping in a Welch (unpooled) SE restores calibration to 0.033-0.038 across all four stress cases. Also: define_froi's argsort-reverse ranking puts NaN first, so a localizer with any non-finite vertex returns an fROI composed entirely of dead vertices (demonstrated exactly), and event_locked_response indexes rows as TRs while ops/source-of-truth.md:52,89 verifies the model returns (n_kept_segments, n_vertices) with empty segments dropped.
maths.search_failures: Two Bash calls exceeded the 120 s foreground limit and were moved to background; both completed with exit code 0 and I read their full output (seed-sensitivity sweep of detection_floor, and the 800-replicate Type I baseline). No search or test was killed or truncated. One genuine failure to report: `np.load('data/algonauts/sub-01_ood_fmri_samples.npy', allow_pickle=False)` errored with "Object arrays cannot be loaded when allow_pickle=False", so I could NOT check the project's real arrays for NaN or zero-variance vertices. Findings 2 and 5 therefore demonstrate the NaN/zero-variance code paths on synthetic input only; I have not established how often TRIBE's actual predictions contain non-finite or constant vertices, and that premise should be checked against a real prediction cache before prioritising those two.

findings.title: glm_contrast_z uses a pooled (equal-variance) SE; at unequal n its permutation test is not level-alpha in either direction
findings.claim: The standard error is Student's POOLED two-sample SE, which assumes the two conditions have equal across-observation variance. That assumption is harmless at equal n (permutation tests are famously robust there) but fails badly at unequal n. Because the resulting statistic is not asymptotically pivotal, wrapping it in a permutation test does NOT rescue it (Behrens-Fisher; cf. Janssen 1997, Chung & Romano 2013 on studentised permutation tests). The MASTER-PLAN S2 design is faces (n>=50) versus the pooled other categories (n>=200) - unequal n by 1:4, with the pooled 'other' arm heterogeneous by construction - which is precisely the configuration that breaks.
findings.evidence: Line 339-340: `var = ((na - 1) * av.var(axis=0, ddof=1) + (nb - 1) * bv.var(axis=0, ddof=1)) / (na + nb - 2)` then `se = np.sqrt(var * (1.0 / na + 1.0 / nb))`. I confirmed this is exactly Student's pooled t, not Welch: it reproduces scipy.stats.ttest_ind(..., equal_var=True) to <=2.2e-16 at (na,nb) = (5,5), (4,12), (12,4), (2,30), (15,15). Measured Type I error of the permutation test on glm_contrast_z (the exact test used at scripts/detection_floor_table.py:76-83), na=50 vs nb=200, V=58, equicorrelated vertices rho=0.6, TRUE MEANS IDENTICAL, nominal one-sided alpha=0.025, n_perm=400, 800 replicates: sd_a/sd_b=1.00 -> 0.0225 +/- 0.0052 (calibrated); sd_a/sd_b=1.50 -> 0.0650 +/- 0.0087 (2.6x nominal, 4.6 SE above); sd_a/sd_b=0.67 -> 0.0050 +/- 0.0025 (5x deflated). Pushed harder (400 reps, n_perm=300): sd ratio 3:1 -> Type I 0.1250; ratio 1:3 -> Type I 0.0000, i.e. the test can never reject at any effect size. Equal n is immune: na=nb=15 with a 1:3 sd ratio gives Type I 0.0250. Replacing only the SE with Welch, se = sqrt(var_a/na + var_b/nb), restores calibration at 50v200 across all four stress cases: 0.0325, 0.0375, 0.0325, 0.0350.
findings.concrete_failure: S2 runs glm_contrast_z(faces_50xV, others_200xV, ffc_verts) and permutes it. Case A - faces are the more variable arm by 1.5x (plausible: fLoc face exemplars vary in viewpoint/identity while the pooled others average out): the test rejects a TRUE NULL 6.5% of the time at nominal 2.5%, and the paper publishes 'TRIBE has a face-selective FFA' off a false positive. Case B - the pooled four-category 'other' arm is the more variable one by 1.5x (the likelier case, since pooling heterogeneous categories inflates variance): Type I drops to 0.005 and at a 3:1 ratio to exactly 0.000, so the statistic reports NO-GO no matter how large the real face effect is. That is the same class of error as the retracted 2026-07-31 spatial_z result - a NO-GO manufactured by the normaliser rather than by the data - reached by a different route, in the statistic built to replace it.
findings.fix: Replace the pooled variance with a Welch (unpooled) SE: `se = np.sqrt(av.var(axis=0, ddof=1) / na + bv.var(axis=0, ddof=1) / nb)`, deleting the `var = ...` pooling line. This is the studentised-permutation form and is asymptotically pivotal, so the surrounding permutation test becomes approximately exact under heteroscedasticity; I verified it restores Type I to 0.033-0.038 at 50v200 for sd ratios 2:1 through 1:3. It is identical to the current code when na == nb and the variances match, so no existing test changes meaning. Additionally, add a test that pins Type I at unequal n with unequal variance, and update ops/interface-contracts.md per CLAUDE.md rule 2 (the signature is unchanged but the documented statistic is not).

findings.title: define_froi ranks with argsort()[::-1], which sorts NaN to the FRONT - a localizer with dead vertices returns an fROI made entirely of them
findings.claim: np.argsort puts NaN LAST in ascending order; reversing with [::-1] therefore puts NaN FIRST. Any non-finite value in the localizer contrast is treated as the most face-selective vertex in the parcel. There is no isfinite guard anywhere in the function. Separately, on a localizer with no signal at all (all selectivity values tied) the same line silently returns the highest-index vertices of the parcel rather than raising - so a broken or empty localizer still produces a confident-looking fROI.
findings.evidence: Line 387-389: `sel = a[pv] - b[pv]` then `keep = pv[np.argsort(sel)[::-1][:k]]`. Run: loc_a with ten genuinely selective vertices at indices 100-109 (value 1.0) and ten NaN vertices at 150-159, loc_b all zeros, parcel = arange(100,200), top_n=10. define_froi returns [150, 151, 152, 153, 154, 155, 156, 157, 158, 159] - the NaN vertices - and none of the ten real ones. Separately, define_froi(np.zeros(200), np.zeros(200), np.arange(100,200), top_n=8) returns [192, 193, 194, 195, 196, 197, 198, 199] with no error. The existing tests (test_define_froi_picks_the_selective_vertices, test_define_froi_caps_at_parcel_size) use only clean finite inputs and do not catch either case.
findings.concrete_failure: S2 defines the face fROI from half the localizer exemplars and tests on the other half. If the localizer half contains any vertex where TRIBE emitted NaN or where the medial-wall mask left non-finite values, the fROI becomes those dead vertices. The subsequent held-out contrast is then computed over vertices that carry no signal, returns a null, and the paper reports 'no face selectivity in a properly defined fROI' - a headline null caused entirely by a sort-order artifact, with the double-dipping safeguard in the docstring providing false reassurance that the ROI definition was done correctly.
findings.fix: Guard before ranking: `finite = np.isfinite(sel)`; if not finite.all(), either raise ValueError naming the offending vertex count or restrict pv/sel to the finite subset and reduce k accordingly (raise if fewer than top_n finite vertices remain). Also raise when the k-th and (k+1)-th selectivity values are exactly equal to the maximum-tie value across the whole parcel (a flat localizer), rather than returning an arbitrary index-ordered subset. Add both as tests.

findings.title: event_locked_response indexes prediction rows as if they were TRs, but predict() returns (n_kept_segments, n_vertices) with empty segments dropped
findings.claim: The function computes `rows = onsets_tr + lag_trs` and indexes `p[rows]` directly, treating row index as TR index. ops/source-of-truth.md verifies that TRIBE v2's predict() returns (n_kept_segments, n_vertices) and that segments with no events are removed by default, so row index and TR index differ by however many segments were dropped before that point. The only guard present is a bounds check; a misalignment leaves rows in range and is therefore completely silent - the exact silent-failure class the docstring says it is guarding against.
findings.evidence: Lines 268-276: `rows = np.asarray(list(onsets_tr), dtype=int) + int(lag_trs)` ... `if rows.min() < 0 or rows.max() >= p.shape[0]: raise IndexError(...)` ... `return p[rows][:, verts].mean(axis=1)`. Against ops/source-of-truth.md line 89 (`Segments with no events are removed by default (remove_empty_segments=True) | VERIFIED | demo_utils.py:148, 370-376`) and line 52 (`A 10 s clip therefore yields ~11 rows of a 100 s window => ~90% of the model window is exact zeros | VERIFIED`), which together establish that the returned array is compacted, not TR-indexed. CLAUDE.md's Data Shapes section repeats this: 'n_kept_segments != n_total_segments - empty segments are dropped'. TR = 1.0 s is verified (source-of-truth line 49), so lag_trs=5 really is 5 s - the lag arithmetic itself is right; only the row->TR identification is wrong. Confirmed by grep that there is currently no production caller (only tests/test_roi_stats.py:244,252), so this is latent, not yet biting.
findings.concrete_failure: S2's localizer is 1 s image on / 8 s ISI. If the blank ISI segments carry no Audio/Video events they are dropped, so a stimulus at true TR 90 (the 11th event) lands at row ~10 in the returned array. event_locked_response(preds, verts, onsets_tr=[0,9,18,...,90], lag_trs=5) reads row 95, which is either off the end (loud) or, for a longer run, a completely unrelated event (silent). Every category mean is then computed from the wrong events, event_locked_contrast returns noise, and the FFA/PPA/EBA/VWFA replication - the paper's positive control against Meta's published result - fails for a reason that looks like a model failure and will be reported as one.
findings.fix: Do not accept a bare array. Either (a) take the `all_segments` list that predict() returns alongside preds and resolve each onset to its row via the segment start times, raising if an onset falls in a dropped segment; or (b) require the caller to pass an explicit `n_trs` and assert `preds.shape[0] == n_trs`, so a compacted array fails loudly instead of silently misaligning. Record the chosen contract in ops/interface-contracts.md before S2 is written.

findings.title: glm_contrast_z is documented and named as a z-score but its null SD ranges from 0.14 to 1.06 depending only on inter-vertex correlation
findings.claim: The ROI value is the arithmetic mean of V per-vertex t-statistics. Under the null its variance is approximately (rho_bar + (1 - rho_bar)/V) * df/(df-2), where rho_bar is the mean inter-vertex correlation of the noise - a nuisance parameter with nothing to do with the effect. The returned number is therefore not on the z scale and cannot be thresholded at 1.96, converted through the normal CDF, or compared numerically to the per-vertex z values in Meta's Fig 4, even though the docstring says it is 'What Meta's Fig 4 actually reports'. Today it is only ever consumed inside a permutation test (scripts/detection_floor_table.py:76-83), which calibrates it, so no wrong number is currently produced - this is a trap set for S2, where MASTER-PLAN says 'Also compute glm_contrast_z. Report both.'
findings.evidence: Measured null distribution of glm_contrast_z with V=58 (the FFCr parcel size), na=nb=15, equicorrelated Gaussian vertices, 4000 replicates per point, true means identical: rho=0.00 -> null SD 0.136, P(|stat|>1.96)=0.0000; rho=0.20 -> 0.483, 0.0000; rho=0.50 -> 0.748, 0.0092; rho=0.80 -> 0.944, 0.0355; rho=0.95 -> 1.029, 0.0520; rho=1.00 -> 1.057, 0.0617. The false-positive rate of a 1.96 threshold thus swings from 0.0000 to 0.062 with rho alone. Null mean stays at 0.00 throughout, so the statistic is unbiased - it is only the scale that is undefined. (Note the accompanying negative result: this is NOT a power pathology. For a uniform effect, mean-of-t and t-of-ROI-mean have identical SNR to first order, both delta*sqrt(n/2)/(sigma*sqrt(rho+(1-rho)/V)), and mean-of-t is better under heteroscedastic per-vertex noise. The brief's 'known pathology when vertices are strongly correlated' is real but is purely about calibration, not sensitivity.)
findings.concrete_failure: S2 reports glm_contrast_z for FFC-right, PPA, EBA, VWFA and V1 and compares the values to Meta's Fig 4 z-map, or applies a z>1.96 / z>3.1 threshold. With realistic TRIBE prediction correlation the ROI statistic's null width is well under 1, so every ROI reads as sub-threshold and the paper concludes 'no category selectivity survives correction' when the permutation test on the same numbers would have rejected. Conversely if a reader assumes null SD 1 and rho happens to be near 1, the nominal 5% is really 6.2%.
findings.fix: Rename to make the scale explicit (e.g. glm_contrast_meant or roi_mean_t) or, better, return the ROI-level studentised statistic instead of the mean of per-vertex ones. At minimum add a hard warning to the docstring: 'The returned value is a mean of per-vertex t-statistics. Its null SD is approximately sqrt(rho_bar) and is NOT 1. It must be calibrated by permutation; never threshold it at a normal quantile and never compare it numerically to a published per-vertex z-map.' Pin the measured null SDs above in a test so the property cannot be forgotten.

findings.title: glm_contrast_z silently scores non-finite and perfectly-separating vertices as z = 0, attenuating the ROI statistic toward the null with no warning
findings.claim: The mask `ok = se > 0` is False for NaN (NaN > 0 evaluates False without warning), so any vertex with non-finite data contributes exactly 0 to the ROI mean instead of propagating NaN or raising. The same line also maps the opposite extreme to 0: a vertex that is constant within each condition but differs between them (se = 0, diff != 0) is infinitely significant and is scored as null. Both directions bias the ROI statistic toward zero, i.e. toward a NO-GO, and both are completely silent - no warning, no error, no NaN in the output.
findings.evidence: Lines 341-344: `z = np.zeros_like(diff)` / `ok = se > 0` / `z[ok] = diff[ok] / se[ok]` / `return float(z.mean())`. Run with warnings.simplefilter('error') to prove silence: a 5-vertex ROI where vertex 2 is all-NaN in condition A returns 17.7924 with no warning and no error; the identical ROI with that vertex removed returns 22.2405 - a 20.0% attenuation from one bad vertex out of five, exactly the (V-1)/V dilution. Second case: a 4-vertex ROI where vertex 0 is constant 5.0 in A and constant 0.0 in B (se=0, perfect separation) returns 13.0917; dropping that vertex returns 17.4556 - the most significant vertex in the ROI drags the mean DOWN because it is scored as zero. The docstring at line 322 admits only the second case ('Vertices with zero pooled variance contribute 0 rather than inf') and does not mention non-finite input at all.
findings.concrete_failure: A real 58-vertex FFCr ROI in which 12 vertices fall on the medial wall or are otherwise emitted as NaN by the model returns an ROI statistic attenuated by 12/58 = 21% relative to the truth, with nothing in the output or logs indicating that a fifth of the ROI was discarded. A borderline result at the D-3 detection floor flips from detected to NO-GO purely from unreported data loss. (Caveat: I could not verify how often TRIBE predictions actually contain non-finite vertices - see search_failures - so the code path is proven but its real-world frequency is not.)
findings.fix: Split the two cases. Raise (or return NaN) on non-finite input: `if not np.isfinite(av).all() or not np.isfinite(bv).all(): raise ValueError(...)`. For the genuine se == 0 case, keep contributing 0 only when diff is also 0, and raise or warn with a vertex count when diff != 0. Return the count of excluded vertices alongside the statistic, or at minimum log it, so silent attenuation is impossible.

findings.title: detection_floor reports a solvable configuration error as a scientific conclusion when alpha < 1/(n_perm+1)
findings.claim: achieved_power calls mc_perm_p, whose smallest possible return value is 1/(n_perm+1). If alpha is below that, no effect size of any magnitude can ever clear the threshold, so the doubling loop runs all the way to max_effect and raises a RuntimeError whose text asserts that the DESIGN is underpowered and instructs the researcher to report that. The design may in fact be perfectly well powered; the only thing wrong is n_perm. There is no validation of alpha against 1/(n_perm+1) anywhere in the function.
findings.evidence: Line 441 `mc_perm_p(a, b, n_perm=n_perm, seed=...)` returns `(ge + 1) / (n_perm + 1)` (line 160), minimum 1/(n_perm+1). Lines 447-454 raise RuntimeError with the message 'the design is underpowered for any plausible effect; report that, do not run it'. Demonstrated: `detection_floor(30, noise_sd=1.0, alpha=0.004, n_sim=5, n_perm=200)` raises after 0.3 s with 'no effect below 1000000.0 reaches 80% power at n=30, sd=1.0, alpha=0.004 - the design is underpowered for any plausible effect; report that, do not run it'. The true analytic MDE for n=30 per group at alpha=0.004 is about 0.79 sd - the design is fine. The trigger is simply 1/(200+1) = 0.004975 > 0.004. With the default n_perm=400 the boundary is 0.0024938, so Bonferroni over 11 or more tests at 0.025 crosses it.
findings.concrete_failure: The operator computes floors for 5 ROIs x 2 IUT contrasts = 10 tests and Bonferroni-corrects to alpha = 0.0025 with n_perm=400 (boundary 0.0024938 - it passes by 6e-7). Adding a sixth ROI takes alpha to 0.00208, below the boundary, and detection_floor raises. The message says the design cannot detect any plausible effect, so - following its own instruction 'report that' - the paper states the design is hopeless when the real fix is n_perm=1000. This is the project's own D-3 doctrine ('no verdict without a floor') producing a false verdict.
findings.fix: Validate up front: `if alpha <= 1.0 / (n_perm + 1): raise ValueError(f"alpha={alpha} is at or below the smallest p-value mc_perm_p can return, 1/(n_perm+1)={1/(n_perm+1):.6f}; increase n_perm to at least {int(np.ceil(1/alpha))}")`. Fail immediately with the actionable message instead of after ~21 doublings with a misleading one.

findings.title: event_locked_contrast silently drops empty other-category arrays, changing the baseline denominator without notice
findings.claim: The comprehension `others = [o for o in others if o.size]` removes any category whose response array arrived empty. Because the baseline is the mean over categories, dropping one silently changes the estimand from 'mean of K category means' to 'mean of K-1 category means'. The function raises only if ALL categories are empty. An upstream failure that loses one category therefore produces a plausible-looking number rather than an error.
findings.evidence: Line 300: `others = [o for o in others if o.size]`, then line 303 `return float(tgt.mean() - np.mean([o.mean() for o in others]))`. Run: event_locked_contrast([10., 10.], [[0., 0.], [4., 4.]]) = 8.0 (baseline = mean(0, 4) = 2). event_locked_contrast([10., 10.], [[], [4., 4.]]) = 6.0 (baseline = 4) - a 25% change in the contrast, returned with no warning. The docstring states the estimand as 'mean(target) - mean over categories of mean(category)' and says nothing about dropping categories.
findings.concrete_failure: S2's protocol is faces minus the mean of bodies/places/objects/characters. If the character category's onsets are lost upstream (a manifest typo, a dropped-segment IndexError swallowed by a caller, a category with all onsets outside the window), event_locked_contrast returns the faces-minus-three-categories contrast. Since characters/VWFA is the lowest-responding category in FFC, dropping it raises the baseline and shrinks the face contrast, biasing toward NO-GO. Nothing in the output distinguishes this from a genuine result.
findings.fix: Raise instead of filtering: `if any(o.size == 0 for o in others): raise ValueError(f"{sum(o.size == 0 for o in others)} of {len(others)} other-category arrays are empty - the baseline is the mean over CATEGORIES, so a missing category silently changes the estimand")`. If a caller genuinely needs the permissive behaviour, make it an explicit opt-in argument and return the surviving category count.

diff.lane_summary:
I ran a numerical differential test between the shipped `event_locked_response`/`event_locked_contrast` in /home/deveshb/workspace/AI/tribe-bench/tribe_tools/roi_stats.py (lines 235-303) and the blind independent implementation (written to /tmp/claude-1065/-home-deveshb-workspace-AI/7dc6b8d5-e29d-4168-a36d-1410e255f4d0/scratchpad/blind_impl.py, harness at .../diff_harness.py, targeted probes at .../probe.py).

HEADLINE: on every well-formed input the two implementations agree to the last bit. 3,000 randomised `event_locked_response` calls (n_trs 6-400, n_vertices 2-300, ROI size 1-80, 1-19 onsets, lag 0-8, preds in both float32 and float64) produced 2,994 evaluated cases and zero numerical or shape disagreements at atol=1e-9; the remaining 6 were skipped by the generator's own range guard. 3,000 randomised `event_locked_contrast` calls (K=1-5 other categories, 1-14 exemplars each, deliberately unequal counts -- max |macro-micro| across the sweep was 0.688, so the estimator choice was genuinely exercised) also agreed exactly. A 20,484-vertex float32 ROI gave a max abs difference of 0.0, because the shipped code does `np.asarray(preds, dtype=float)` and therefore also accumulates in float64 -- the blind author's predicted ~1e-7 dtype divergence (their caveat 7) does not occur.

THE CENTRAL AMBIGUITY IS NOT A DISAGREEMENT. The blind author flagged macro-vs-micro baseline as the first thing to check. Both implementations use MACRO (unweighted mean of per-category means). On a realistic 1 s-flash / 8 s-ISI / +5 s-read simulation with unequal exemplar counts (faces 6, objects 10, scenes 4, bodies 3) both returned 0.600835469 against an analytic macro of 0.600000 and a micro of 0.612738 -- difference 0.0e+00. Two independent readings of the published protocol converged on the same estimator, which is real corroborating evidence that faces > (objects+scenes+bodies)/3 is the right contrast vector.

Every disagreement found is therefore behavioural, at the input-validation boundary, and in every substantive case the shipped implementation is the permissive one that returns a plausible-looking wrong number where the blind one raises -- precisely the silent-failure class this codebase names as its signature bug. I report 7 shipped-side gaps (4 of which produce a silently corrupted scientific quantity) and 1 case where the blind implementation is the over-strict/wrong one. Neither function has a production caller yet -- a scoped grep over scripts/, neurocheck/, brainlens/, tribe_tools/, tests/ finds only tests/test_roi_stats.py -- so these are latent, cheap to fix now, and expensive after the Gate 0 / NeuroCheck harness starts calling them (roi_stats.py:43 designates `event_locked_contrast` as the D027 primary statistic). The existing suite (26 tests) passes; none of these paths is covered.
diff.search_failures: None. Every command completed cleanly with a normal exit status. The one non-zero exit was an intentional IndexError inside my own probe script (a badly-chosen ROI size in probe P2), which I diagnosed and corrected in the same script; it was not a tool or search failure. findings.title: event_locked_contrast silently drops empty other-categories, changing the divisor K and returning a different contrast than the one requested
findings.claim: Line 300 filters zero-length categories out of `other_responses` with no warning. The baseline then averages over K-1 (or fewer) categories while the caller believes it averaged over K. The published contrast faces > (objects+scenes+bodies)/3 silently becomes faces > (objects+scenes)/2, and nothing in the return value, the type, or the logs marks the substitution. The blind implementation raises ValueError here.
findings.evidence:
roi_stats.py:299-303:
    others = [np.asarray(list(o), dtype=float) for o in other_responses]
    others = [o for o in others if o.size]
    if not others:
        raise ValueError("event_locked_contrast needs at least one other category")
    return float(tgt.mean() - np.mean([o.mean() for o in others]))
The `if o.size` filter is the whole bug: it converts 'a category has no events' from an error into a silent change of estimator. The docstring one line above (roi_stats.py:285-288) promises 'each category is averaged first, then those category means are averaged' and says nothing about dropping categories.
findings.concrete_failure:
faces=[1.0,1.0,1.0], objects=[0.0,0.0], scenes=[0.9,0.9], bodies=np.array([]) (every bodies event fell off the end of the run, or the bodies condition was filtered upstream).
  shipped -> 0.55   (baseline = mean(0.0, 0.9) = 0.45, K silently became 2)
  intended -> 0.70  (baseline = mean(0.0, 0.9, 0.0) = 0.30, K = 3)
  blind -> ValueError: other_responses[2] is empty; a category with zero exemplars has no mean
A 27% inflation of the face-selectivity contrast, with no error, no warning, and no change in return type. Because this is the D027 primary statistic feeding Gate 0's GO/NO-GO rule, an empty category produced by any upstream filter (an out-of-range read, a dropped segment, a per-category exclusion) can flip a NO-GO to a GO on a number that was never computed the way the protocol specifies.
findings.fix: Delete the `others = [o for o in others if o.size]` filter and raise instead: `for i, o in enumerate(others):\n    if o.size == 0:\n        raise ValueError(f"other_responses[{i}] has zero exemplars; the baseline divisor K would silently change")`. Keep the existing `if not others` check for a genuinely empty sequence.

findings.title: event_locked_response truncates non-integral onsets toward zero instead of rejecting them, reading the wrong TR and mis-measuring the HRF amplitude by ~29%
findings.claim: Line 268 coerces onsets with `np.asarray(..., dtype=int)`, which truncates toward zero rather than rounding or raising. An onset carried as a float in seconds -- the natural form, since TR = 1.0 s makes seconds and row indices numerically equal -- loses up to a full TR. `int(lag_trs)` on the same line truncates the lag identically. The blind implementation accepts exactly-integral floats and raises ValueError on anything else.
findings.evidence:
roi_stats.py:268:
    rows = np.asarray(list(onsets_tr), dtype=int) + int(lag_trs)
NumPy's int cast truncates: np.asarray([2.7], dtype=int) -> 2, and np.asarray([4.0 - 1e-9], dtype=int) -> 3. Likewise int(5.9) -> 5 and int(-0.5) -> 0. Nothing warns.
findings.concrete_failure:
Simulated double-gamma HRF at TR=1.0 s, six events at 8 s ISI (onsets 4,12,20,28,36,44 s), lag_trs=5, ROI mean over 10 vertices:
  exact integer onsets -> [0.146206, 0.136198, 0.118143, 0.117078, 0.117061, 0.117061]
  same onsets as floats carrying 1e-9 of representation error -> [0.104194, 0.110673, 0.088260, 0.086609, 0.086578, 0.086578]
  relative amplitude error on event 1: 28.73%
The truncated call reads t+4 s instead of t+5 s, i.e. off the HRF peak onto its rising flank, for EVERY event -- a systematic, direction-preserving amplitude loss that looks like a weak-but-real effect rather than a bug. A stimulus log entry at 10.6 s reads row 15 (t+4.4 s) where the nearest row is 16. Blind raises ValueError. Fractional lag_trs=5.5 and 5.9 both silently become lag 5, and lag_trs=-0.5 silently becomes lag 0.
findings.fix:
Validate before casting. Accept integers and exactly-integral floats, reject the rest: `o = np.asarray(list(onsets_tr), dtype=float)
if not np.all(o == np.rint(o)):
    raise ValueError(f"onsets_tr must be whole TRs; got non-integral values {o[o != np.rint(o)][:5].tolist()}")
rows = np.rint(o).astype(int) + _int_lag(lag_trs)` with the same integrality check applied to lag_trs. Do not substitute rounding for truncation -- silently rounding is the same class of bug with a smaller constant.

findings.title: NaN/inf at the read positions propagate silently through both functions and then deflate the Mann-Whitney U statistic without raising
findings.claim: Neither function checks for non-finite values. A single NaN in preds at one (event row, ROI vertex) position makes that event's entire ROI mean NaN; the NaN then flows into event_locked_contrast (also unchecked) and into u_statistic/exact_perm_p, where IEEE comparison semantics make every NaN comparison False so the NaN contributes 0 to U instead of erroring. The blind implementation raises ValueError at both stages.
findings.evidence:
roi_stats.py:276: `return p[rows][:, verts].mean(axis=1)` -- plain mean, no finite check.
roi_stats.py:303: `return float(tgt.mean() - np.mean([o.mean() for o in others]))` -- same.
roi_stats.py:76-82, u_statistic: `if f > s: u += 1.0 elif f == s: u += 0.5` -- with f = NaN both branches are False, so the pair silently scores 0 rather than being flagged.
findings.concrete_failure:
preds 20x8, ROI [1,2,3], onset 0, lag 5, with preds[5,2] = np.nan:
  shipped -> array([nan])   blind -> ValueError
Carried downstream: face_vals = [1.0, 1.2, nan, 1.1] vs other_vals = [0.1, 0.2, 0.15, 0.05], which is perfect separation apart from the NaN.
  u_statistic -> 12.0 instead of 16.0 (max)
  exact_perm_p -> 0.0286 instead of 0.0143
At Gate 0's alpha = 0.025 (iut_pass default, roi_stats.py:171) that is the difference between PASS and FAIL. One NaN vertex in one event silently converts a perfectly separating, significant face-selectivity result into a non-significant one, and the NaN never surfaces as an error anywhere in the chain.
findings.fix: Check only the positions actually read, so NaNs elsewhere in preds stay the caller's business: after slicing, `block = p[rows][:, verts]`, add `if not np.all(np.isfinite(block)): raise ValueError(f"preds has {int((~np.isfinite(block)).sum())} non-finite value(s) at the requested (event row, ROI vertex) positions")`. Add the equivalent check to event_locked_contrast on tgt and on each category. Do not switch to nanmean -- that would average each event over a different, unstated vertex subset.

findings.title: An all-False boolean ROI mask bypasses the empty-ROI guard and returns NaN, because len() of a mask is the vertex count, not the ROI size
findings.claim: The guard at line 267 is `len(verts) == 0`. For a boolean mask, len() is n_vertices regardless of how many vertices are selected, so an all-False mask sails past the guard, `p[rows][:, verts]` yields shape (n_events, 0), and `.mean(axis=1)` returns NaN with only a RuntimeWarning. The guard that exists specifically to catch an empty ROI does not catch the empty ROI. Blind raises TypeError on boolean verts.
findings.concrete_failure: An fROI built by thresholding (define_froi-style selection, or `parcel_mask & (selectivity > thresh)`) that selects zero vertices for one subject or one ROI: event_locked_response returns an array of NaN instead of raising 'empty ROI vertex set'. Those NaNs then reach u_statistic and silently deflate U (see the NaN finding), so an ROI that was never actually defined contributes a spurious non-significant result to the Gate 0 table rather than an error the operator would see.

findings.title: Negative vertex indices wrap silently to the opposite hemisphere instead of raising
findings.claim: verts is passed straight to NumPy fancy indexing with no range check, so a negative index wraps to the end of the vertex axis and returns a real number from the wrong brain region. Onsets get a two-sided range check (line 271) but vertices get none. Blind raises IndexError for any vertex outside [0, n_vertices).
findings.concrete_failure: On the documented fsaverage5 layout (CLAUDE.md: left hemisphere 0..N-1, right hemisphere N..2N-1, 20484 total), a right-hemisphere ROI built by an off-by-one or by a sentinel -1 in an atlas lookup silently reads the last right-hemisphere vertex. For a bilateral or contralateral-control ROI the wrapped index lands in the opposite hemisphere entirely: the function returns a well-formed float for an ROI that does not exist, and the contrast, the U statistic and the p-value all proceed normally on a region that was never measured.
findings.fix:
Bounds-check the vertex axis symmetrically with the row axis, before the slice: `v = np.asarray(verts, dtype=int)
bad = v[(v < 0) | (v >= p.shape[1])]
if bad.size:
    raise IndexError(f"verts contains indices outside [0, {p.shape[1]}): {np.unique(bad)[:20].tolist()}")`. Checking the low side matters as much as the high side -- the high side already errors, the low side is the silent one.

findings.title: Duplicate ROI vertex indices silently over-weight those vertices in the ROI mean
findings.claim: A repeated index in verts is read twice and counted twice in the mean, producing an undeclared weighted average rather than the mean over the ROI's vertex set that the docstring promises. Blind raises ValueError. The blind author predicted (their caveat 4) that this is the check most likely to differ, and it is.
findings.evidence:
roi_stats.py:276: `return p[rows][:, verts].mean(axis=1)` -- fancy indexing with a repeated index yields a repeated column; `.mean(axis=1)` divides by len(verts), not by the number of distinct vertices.
Measured on preds = arange(160).reshape(20,8), onset 0, lag 5: verts=[1,1,2] -> 41.3333, verts=[1,2] -> 41.5. The docstring (roi_stats.py:241) calls the result the 'ROI response', and a set of vertices has no duplicates.
findings.concrete_failure: An ROI assembled by concatenating overlapping sources -- e.g. np.concatenate([glasser_ffc_verts, froi_verts]) where the fROI was selected from inside the parcel, or a bilateral ROI built by unioning two parcel lists that share a boundary vertex -- double-weights every vertex in the overlap. With a 58-vertex right-FFC parcel and a ~104-vertex fROI drawn from it (the sizes named in define_froi's docstring, roi_stats.py:347-357), most of the ROI would be doubled, biasing the contrast toward whatever the overlap region does. No error, no warning, and the bias is invisible in the output.
findings.fix: Either raise -- `u, c = np.unique(v, return_counts=True)\nif u.size != v.size:\n    raise ValueError(f"verts contains duplicated indices {u[c>1][:20].tolist()}; duplicates silently over-weight the ROI mean")` -- or, if a weighted ROI is ever wanted, expose it as an explicit `weights=` parameter. Silent de-duplication is the one option to avoid: it changes the caller's stated ROI without telling them.

findings.title: A 2-D onsets_tr array returns a silently wrong-shaped result instead of raising
findings.claim: onsets_tr is never checked for dimensionality. A 2-D onsets array makes `rows` 2-D, `p[rows]` 3-D, and `[:, verts]` then indexes the wrong axis, so `.mean(axis=1)` averages over events rather than over ROI vertices and returns a (n_blocks, n_vertices) array. The docstring promises (n_events,). Blind raises ValueError on any non-1-D onsets.
findings.evidence:
roi_stats.py:268-276: `rows = np.asarray(list(onsets_tr), dtype=int) + int(lag_trs)` ... `return p[rows][:, verts].mean(axis=1)`. Neither `rows.ndim` nor the output shape is asserted; the only shape guard in the function is `p.ndim != 2` on line 264.
Measured: preds (20,8), verts=[1,2], onsets_tr=[[0,1,2],[3,4,5]] -> shipped returns shape (2, 8) containing raw per-vertex values [[52..59],[76..83]], i.e. neither an ROI mean nor one value per event. Blind -> ValueError: onsets_tr must be 1-D (or a scalar); got shape (2, 3).
findings.concrete_failure: Onsets held per-block or per-run as a rectangular (n_blocks, n_events_per_block) array -- a natural layout for a blocked localizer with 1 s flashes at 8 s ISI -- are passed in without a .ravel(). The function returns an array of the wrong shape and the wrong quantity. Whether that surfaces depends entirely on ROI size versus block count: with len(verts) > n_blocks it happens to raise an unrelated IndexError, but whenever len(verts) <= n_blocks it returns silently. The failure is therefore data-dependent and will not show up in a small test.
findings.fix: Assert the shape right after building rows: `rows = np.atleast_1d(rows)\nif rows.ndim != 1:\n    raise ValueError(f"onsets_tr must be 1-D (one entry per event); got shape {rows.shape}")`. Two lines, and it also makes the promised (n_events,) return shape true by construction.

findings.title: Blind implementation is over-strict on negative onsets whose read row is genuinely inside the run -- here the shipped behaviour is the correct one
findings.claim: The blind implementation rejects any negative onset outright, justifying it (its decision D2) as preventing NumPy negative-index wraparound. But the shipped implementation range-checks the computed ROW, not the onset, so no wraparound is possible: onset = -3 with lag 5 yields row 2, a legitimate in-range read of the response 5 s after an event that began before the recording window. The blind implementation is the wrong one on this case.
findings.evidence:
blind_impl.py, event_locked_response:
    if np.any(onsets < 0):
        raise IndexError(f"onsets_tr contains negative onset row(s) {bad}; negative indices would wrap around to the end of the run under NumPy indexing")
This fires before the row is ever computed. The stated rationale does not hold against the shipped design, roi_stats.py:271:
    if rows.min() < 0 or rows.max() >= p.shape[0]:
        raise IndexError(...)
which already makes a negative row impossible. Measured on preds (20,8), verts [1,2,3], onset -3, lag 5: shipped -> 18.0, exactly mean(preds[2, [1,2,3]]) = 18.0, the arithmetically correct answer. Blind -> IndexError. The two agree (both raise) on onset -8, where the row really is negative.
findings.concrete_failure: A localizer run trimmed at the start (dummy-scan removal, or a segment-alignment offset per the source-of-truth warning that predict() drops empty segments) shifts every onset by a constant, putting the first event's onset at a negative row while its +5 s read still lands inside the retained data. The blind implementation refuses the whole call; the shipped one correctly returns the response for that event. Adopting blind's rule verbatim would discard the first event of every trimmed run.
findings.fix: Do not port blind's negative-onset rejection into roi_stats.py. Keep the shipped row-level range check, which is the correct and sufficient guard. If a diagnostic is wanted, log rather than raise: a negative onset with an in-range row often indicates an unapplied time offset and is worth noting, but it is not an error and must not drop the event.

diff.lane_summary: Differential test of `event_locked_response` and `event_locked_contrast` in /home/deveshb/workspace/AI/tribe-bench/tribe_tools/roi_stats.py against a blind reimplementation. Scope covered: 399 randomised contiguous-row trials (n_trs 3-200, n_vertices 1-300, ROI size 1-60 with and without duplicate vertices, lag 0-7, 1-12 onsets, float32 and float64 preds) — ZERO numerical disagreement, agreement to <1e-9; plus 300 randomised contrast trials with 1-5 other categories at deliberately unequal exemplar counts — ZERO disagreement, confirming both independently chose the mean-of-category-means baseline (the blind author's ambiguity #1 is settled: shipped agrees, and tests/test_roi_stats.py:371 pins it). The core arithmetic is therefore concordant. Every disagreement found is in the edge/failure surface, and it splits cleanly: shipped WINS the two semantic disagreements (it resolves rows by absolute time rather than row arithmetic, and defaults lag_trs=0 rather than 5 — both correct per ops/source-of-truth.md lines 50-52, and the blind version is wrong on both because its spec conveyed a false `(n_trs, n_vertices)` row==TR model), while shipped LOSES every silent-failure disagreement. Four of those are substantive: a negative vertex index silently reads the opposite hemisphere; `event_locked_contrast` silently deletes empty other-categories and changes the contrast vector's k; NaN flows through to `u_statistic` as a lost comparison and flips the pre-registered IUT verdict; and `event_locked_response(lag_trs=k)` demands every intermediate row 0..k so it aborts on gapped `predict()` output where the one row it needs exists. `python3 -m pytest tests/test_roi_stats.py -q` -> 32 passed in 4.47s, so none of these are pinned.
diff.search_failures: None. No recursive search was run. One scoped grep over the single exact path tests/test_roi_stats.py completed cleanly; every other file access was by exact absolute path (tribe_tools/roi_stats.py, ops/source-of-truth.md). The pytest run and all Python scripts exited normally with no truncation or kills.

findings.title: Negative vertex index silently reads the opposite hemisphere instead of raising
findings.symbol: peri_event_timecourse / event_locked_response (also spatial_z, raw_roi_mean, roi_minus_reference, glm_contrast_z)
findings.claim: `verts` is validated only for emptiness and then handed straight to NumPy fancy indexing, so a negative index wraps to the end of the vertex axis. Because CLAUDE.md fixes the ordering as left hemisphere 0..N-1 and right hemisphere N..2N-1, a negative ROI index reads the CONTRALATERAL hemisphere and returns a plausible number. The blind implementation raises IndexError on exactly this input, for exactly this stated reason.
findings.evidence: peri_event_timecourse:337-338 `if len(verts) == 0: raise ValueError("empty ROI vertex set")` is the only check, then line 351 `roi = p[:, verts].mean(axis=1)`. Demonstrated on a 20,484-vertex array with left hemisphere set to 1.0 and right to 9.0: honest left ROI [0,1,2,3] -> 1.0; ROI [0,1,2,-1] -> 3.0 (right-hemisphere vertex 20483 averaged in); ROI [-1,-2,-3,-4] -> 9.0, i.e. an entirely right-hemisphere reading, no exception. raw_roi_mean gives 3.0 and spatial_z gives -0.5 on the same ROI. Over-range indices DO raise (both implementations agree); only the negative side is silent.
findings.concrete_failure: A right-FFC ROI built by the documented `left=0, right=+expected_size` offset arithmetic (ops/source-of-truth.md:135), or any parcel lookup that emits -1 for 'unlabeled', yields an ROI containing negative entries. event_locked_response returns a finite number mixing the two hemispheres, the face-selectivity contrast is computed on it, and Gate 0 issues a GO/NO-GO on a region that is partly or wholly the wrong hemisphere. Nothing in the output distinguishes this from a valid run.
findings.fix: In peri_event_timecourse (and the other ROI entry points), after the emptiness check add an explicit range check mirroring the existing loud style: coerce `v = np.asarray(verts)`, and if `np.any(v < 0) | np.any(v >= p.shape[1])`, raise IndexError naming the offending indices, the valid range 0..n_vertices-1, and that negative indices are refused because they silently read the opposite hemisphere.

findings.title: event_locked_contrast silently drops empty other-categories, changing the contrast vector's k
findings.claim: A filter deletes any other-category with zero events before averaging, so a k-category localizer contrast silently becomes a (k-1)-category contrast. The docstring's whole subject is that the baseline is the mean of category means and 'the choice is recorded here so it can be challenged rather than discovered' — but k itself changes without any record. The blind implementation raises ValueError, explicitly refusing to guess a baseline from an empty category.
findings.evidence: Line 452: `others = [o for o in others if o.size]`, then line 455 `np.mean([o.mean() for o in others])`. Measured: `event_locked_contrast(faces=[1.0]*4, [objects=[0.2]*2, bodies=[], scenes=[0.4]*5])` returns 0.700000, which is exactly the k=2 answer 1.0-(0.2+0.4)/2. The declared contrast vector [1,-1/3,-1/3,-1/3] was silently replaced by [1,-1/2,-1/2]. Had bodies actually been measured at 0.9 the answer is 0.500000 — a 0.200 discrepancy with no diagnostic.
findings.concrete_failure: Gate 0 v2's rule is 'faces>objects AND faces>bodies' (iut_pass docstring, line 174). If one clip contributes no body exemplars — a routine outcome once `remove_empty_segments=True` drops rows, or when a category's onsets fall outside the clip — the bodies term vanishes from the baseline and the reported contrast is inflated by the amount that category would have suppressed it. The paper reports a k=3 localizer contrast that was computed as k=2.
findings.fix: Delete the filter. Raise ValueError naming the empty category index, in the same loud style as the surrounding code, so the caller must decide explicitly whether to drop the category (and re-declare k) or fix the onsets. If dropping is ever legitimate it must be an explicit opt-in argument, not a silent default.

findings.title: NaN propagates silently through the contrast into u_statistic as a lost comparison, flipping the pre-registered verdict
findings.claim: Neither event_locked_response nor event_locked_contrast checks for non-finite values, and u_statistic's comparison chain treats NaN as strictly losing every pairwise comparison rather than erroring — `nan > s` is False and `nan == s` is False, so a corrupt clip contributes 0.0 to U instead of raising. The blind implementation raises ValueError at both stages, naming NaN propagation as the reason.
findings.evidence: peri_event_timecourse line 354 `out[:, j] = roi[...]` with no finiteness check; event_locked_contrast line 455 returns `float(tgt.mean() - ...)` which is nan. u_statistic:76-81 `if f > s: u += 1.0 elif f == s: u += 0.5` — no else, so NaN adds 0. Measured on 4v4: face=[0.5,0.4,nan,0.45] vs scene=[0.1,0.12,0.08,0.11] gives U=12.0 and exact_perm_p=0.0286; replacing the NaN with the plausible 0.42 gives U=16.0 (perfect separation) and p=0.0143. iut_pass(0.0286, 0.0286) is False; iut_pass(0.0143, 0.0143) is True.
findings.concrete_failure: One NaN vertex anywhere in one sampled ROI row turns a perfectly separating 4v4 result into a failing one: the pre-registered alpha=0.025 IUT flips from PASS to FAIL and Gate 0 prints NO-GO on data whose only defect is an uncleaned value. The direction is systematic, not random — NaN always loses, so the bias is always toward a false negative, exactly the failure mode the module header calls decision-critical.
findings.fix: Two independent guards. (a) In peri_event_timecourse, after building `out`, raise ValueError if `not np.all(np.isfinite(out))`, reporting the count and the first offending event. (b) In u_statistic, reject non-finite inputs up front rather than letting the comparison chain absorb them, so any future caller path is covered too.

findings.title: event_locked_response(lag_trs=k) requires every intermediate row 0..k and aborts even when the one row it needs exists
findings.claim: event_locked_response is implemented as a wrapper that builds the whole time course from lag 0 to lag k and then discards all but the last column. Because peri_event_timecourse resolves and validates every lag, the call fails if ANY of onset+0 .. onset+k-1 is missing, even though only onset+k is read. On `predict()` output with `remove_empty_segments=True` the row grid is genuinely gappy, so this is a spurious IndexError on analysable data — and it also does k+1 times the necessary work.
findings.evidence: Lines 420-423: `tc = peri_event_timecourse(..., pre_trs=0, post_trs=int(lag_trs)); return tc[:, int(lag_trs)]`, and peri_event_timecourse:353-354 loops `for j, lag in enumerate(lags): out[:, j] = roi[_resolve_rows(rt, onsets + lag)]`, with _resolve_rows raising on the first unresolvable time. Measured with rows present for t=0..11 and t=15..39: `event_locked_response(P, roi, [9.0], keep, lag_trs=6)` raises IndexError complaining about t=12.000, although the row for t=9+6=15 is present at index 12 and the correct return value is 49.5. `lag_trs=0` at the same onset returns 37.5 without complaint. The blind implementation, which touches only the target row, returns a value.
findings.concrete_failure: Reading at any non-zero lag on real predict() output raises whenever a single intervening second happened to be an empty segment. Since ops/source-of-truth.md:52 records that Meta's own demo keeps 53 of 100 segments (and the repo's Kaggle run kept 31), gaps are the norm, not the exception. A lag-sweep via peak_lag_trs is unaffected (it legitimately needs the whole course), but a targeted single-lag read aborts an analysis that the data supports.
findings.fix: Give event_locked_response its own single-lag path: `roi = np.asarray(preds, float)[:, verts].mean(axis=1); return roi[_resolve_rows(row_times_s, np.asarray(onset_times_s, float) + lag_trs)]`, after the same shape/verts/onsets validation peri_event_timecourse performs. That resolves exactly the requested row, keeps the loud IndexError when that row is genuinely absent, and drops the cost from k+1 resolutions to one.

findings.title: Non-integral lag_trs is silently truncated toward zero
findings.claim: `lag_trs` is guarded only against being negative, then passed through `int()` twice, which truncates a fractional lag without comment. The blind implementation raises ValueError on non-integral lags, accepting integral-valued floats only.
findings.evidence: Line 418 `if lag_trs < 0: raise ValueError(...)`, lines 421 and 423 `int(lag_trs)`. Measured: with rows 0..39 and onset 10.0, `lag_trs=5` returns [30.5] and `lag_trs=5.99` also returns [30.5] — the 5.99 request was answered at lag 5. `lag_trs=-0.5` does raise, so the failure is one-sided.
findings.concrete_failure: A caller who computes a lag in seconds and divides by a TR they believe is 0.5 s (the superseded 2 Hz figure that ops/source-of-truth.md:48 marks as WRONG) passes lag_trs=5.99 or 9.98 and receives the lag-5 or lag-9 answer with no indication the request was altered. The docstring insists 'any non-zero value must be justified by a measured peak' — a truncated lag is not the lag that was justified.
findings.fix: Validate before use: reject a non-integral lag_trs with ValueError, accepting integral-valued floats and casting them, mirroring the existing loud-failure convention in this module.

findings.title: Onsets misaligned by exactly half a TR are accepted silently, with ties resolved to the earlier row
findings.claim: The tolerance is 0.5 s while the verified TR is 1.0 s, and the out-of-tolerance test is strict (`err > tol`), so an onset exactly midway between two rows passes at the boundary and is resolved to whichever row the tie-break picks — always the earlier one, because the nearest-row comparison uses `<=`. Every requested time within half a TR of some row therefore resolves, and the maximum silent timing error is exactly half a TR, biased systematically early. The blind implementation rejects any non-integral onset outright.
findings.evidence: Line 278 `tol: float = 0.5`; line 285 `pick = np.where(np.abs(want - left) <= np.abs(right - want), idx - 1, idx)`; line 288 `bad = err > tol`. Measured on rows 0..39: onset 12.0 -> [24.5], onset 12.4999 -> [24.5], onset 12.5 -> [24.5] (the exact tie resolves EARLY, err == tol == 0.5 passes), onset 12.6 -> [26.5].
findings.concrete_failure: With the published design (1 s stimulus, 8 s interval) an onset list computed on a clock offset by 0.5 s from the segment grid resolves cleanly with no warning while every event is read one TR early.         "selectivity — argsort ranks NaN as most selective; clean or mask the localizer first"
